explanations.explanation: This neuron lights up on structural “boilerplate” markers—things like post‐metadata stamps, copyright/legal notices and file‐header lines (dates, “Last edited by…,” “©… All rights reserved,” all-caps warnings, image/file labels, etc.). It’s picking up on the standardized header/footer tokens that frame user content rather than its substantive prose.

This feature lights up on the stereotyped “preface” or boilerplate meta-text at the start of posts or pages—things like apologies (“sorry if this is the wrong forum…”) or placeholder/disclaimer notices (“This is a placeholder page for X…”) that introduce or qualify the content.
This neuron fires on the subordinating conjunction “because” when it introduces a caveat or concessive reason clause (e.g. the “just because X doesn’t mean Y” pattern).

This feature fires on the “.” token when it serves as the closing dot of an abbreviation or initialism (e.g. single‐letter initials like “A.”, titles like “Gov.” or “Sen.”, and multi‐letter acronyms like “U.S.C.”).
This neuron fires on the “.” token when it serves as an abbreviation or sentence-boundary period—i.e. the dot after capitalized or initialism tokens (U.S., Mrs., Inc., St., Jan., Mr., etc.).

This feature fires on the little “headline” or boilerplate opener at the start of a text block—those standalone sentences (often ending in a period or exclamation point) that define scope, give a section title or summary, issue a disclaimer or thank-you, introduce terms or definitions, etc. In other words, it marks the framing/introductory sentence that labels or summarizes the following content.

explanations.explanation: This neuron fires whenever the model encounters a “marked” token – that is, anything that sticks out from ordinary running English text: diff‐markers or quote arrows (+, –, >, >>), section symbols (§), bullet/asterisk lists, soft hyphens, trademark or accent marks, non-English fragments (Arabic, French “c’est”), all‐caps branding, emoji or replacement glyphs, foreign names with apostrophes (O’Hara, O’Donnell), catalog numbers (“144 Margaret…”), product-type labels (“Vinyl”), recipe-style asides (“hmm c’est super bon!!”), etc. In short, it’s detecting typographic/orthographic outliers – punctuation‐heavy, formatting cues or rare domain-specific tokens that signal a shift in register or structure.

This neuron detects typographic/structural markup around key labels—things set off in quotes, parentheses or other delimiters (chapter-numbers in a TOC, section numbers, dates, product names, song/book titles, legal terms, code tokens, etc.) that signal headings, definitions or emphasized list items.

This neuron isn’t tracking any particular meaning or part of speech, but simply the presence of common letter-substrings (trigrams or so) inside tokens. It lights up whenever a frequent three- (or four-) letter sequence (e.g. “ber,” “der,” “ret,” “any,” “eng,” etc.) appears, regardless of whether that fragment sits in a place name, personal name, product term, code keyword, or ordinary English word.

This feature detects front-of-text “lead-in” or heading cues—tokens that introduce or orient a new content block (e.g. “Each,” “Recently,” “Here,” “Welcome,” “Amazing,” “Nov,” “Below”). It marks the opening word of posts, updates or section titles that signal “here’s what’s coming.”

This feature fires on tokens that anchor key factual or summary statements—especially explicit numbers or percentages and discourse markers that introduce conclusions or conditions (e.g. “as far as … concerned,” “as a result,” “as soon as”). In effect, it highlights the points in the text where quantitative data or summary‐of‐result phrasing occurs.
This neuron is a “dot‐in‐abbreviation” detector—it fires on the period in capitalized initials, acronyms, titles or suffixes (e.g. U.S., Gov., M.D., Inc., name initials).

This neuron detects sentence-initial discourse markers—subordinating conjunctions or connective words (For, While, Although, Its, etc.) that open a clause to introduce background, reason, contrast or elaboration. It flags the “hook” at the start of a sentence that signals an explanatory or concessive relationship.

This feature is a sentence-boundary detector: it spikes on sentence-final periods and on the first word of the next sentence (e.g. “Every,” “For,” “Oct,” “Ext,” etc.), marking ends and beginnings of sentences.

A concise way to put it: this neuron lights up on the leading subword of common metadata or section‐label tokens – the prefixes of words like “Average,” “Registration,” “Published,” “Retrieved,” “Dimension,” “Viewed,” “Happened,” etc. – marking document headings or field labels that introduce structured data.
This feature detects the final period at the end of an opening topic‐defining sentence—i.e. the boundary between the initial “topic sentence” or summary statement and the body that follows.

This neuron is a segment‐boundary detector: it lights up on the very first content token of a new text snippet or list item (e.g. “Fab,” “Put,” “Every,” “Its,” etc.) and again on the period that closes that snippet’s opening sentence. It thus flags the start and end of standalone text chunks.

This neuron flags the end‐of‐sentence boundary on a document’s heading or lead‐in line—i.e. the final token (often punctuation or the last word) of a title or opening sentence that introduces a section.

This neuron detects “machine‐readable” reference fragments—URL/URI paths, DOIs, date‐style strings, file‐extensions and other alphanumeric identifiers and codes—i.e. the structural punctuation–digit patterns used for links, citations and technical references.

This neuron fires whenever a sentence uses a little “linking” preposition (to / of / with) that introduces an argument or participant role—e.g. a recipient (“talk to someone”), a subset (“one of them”), or a comitative (“share with you”). It’s basically spotting PP markers that tie an action to its target or member.
